item.content:encoded:
Reading time: 4 minutes

Supernovae are one of the most fascinating phenomena of the universe. Today I will try to give you an approximate idea of what occurs. We will also talk about their importance in the history and development of the elements that make up our cosmos.

What is a supernova?

A supernova is a great explosion produced in the last stages of the life of a very massive star. They are one of the most impressive processes of the universe. To give a general idea, in a common process of these characteristics the energy released can come to be some 100 times higher than that released by our Sun in the last 4,600 million years.

Prior moment: some important ideas about stars.

The first thing that we have to keep in mind is that in a star there are two contributions that oppose each other: the internal pressure due to the internal structure of the star and the gravitational force. Don’t worry about the terminology; the only thing that you have to keep in mind is that: the first pushes the star to expand and the second to contract. In a simple way, what occurs in the moments prior to the supernova is a combination of these two processes. We must also keep in mind that stars can be structured in diverse layers, although in this explanation we will be interested above all in the figure of the core.

The core is the innermost part of the star and where the highest temperatures are concentrated; it is also where many of the most important reactions in the different stages of the life of the star are produced. With this idea of the core we have enough for what follows.

Development of the internal process.

In moments prior to a supernova, in the core of the massive star reactions keep occurring that produce heavier elements, until reaching iron. As iron is the heaviest stable element, the reactions stop and the gravitational force begins to overcome the internal pressure, and it begins to contract; this makes the temperature increase drastically.

In this process the core keeps releasing its energy due to the new reactions that are produced by the high temperatures, and this makes its speed of collapse (of contraction) increase as it cools due to the loss of energy. The contraction is maintained until it reaches a limit where its density reaches levels similar to those of the atomic nucleus, and it becomes rigid, since under these conditions it cannot be compressed any more; this makes the internal part of the core rebound. Finally a pressure wave is formed that expands towards the exterior of the core.

On the other hand, due to the release of energy from the core, the upper parts of the star (where many of the materials that compose it are) also contract rapidly, cooking up the perfect recipe for the final explosion.

The final explosion is produced because the upper layers of the star crash against the core and the pressure wave that was coming out of it. The expansive wave of this crash pushes all the layers of the star outwards. If part of this released energy is converted into light, this explosion can come to have an enormous visibility, and it is this that we really call a supernova.

Importance of supernovae in the universe.

The importance that this process has in the universe is enormous. Elements such as zinc, lead or uranium have not to this day been found to form in processes other than in the moments prior to a supernova. These elements, among others, are key for, for example, our own existence (remember that zinc is an important catalyst in our organism).

To finish we can comment on an expression that perhaps you have heard someone say during your academic stage. Expressions like “we are stardust” or “we are part of a star” are frequently heard in one conference or another. This is because the presence of these materials on Earth makes it possible for us to affirm with great reliability that our solar system formed from the explosion of a dying star that ended up exploding as a supernova 5,000 million years ago.

Author

Miguel Jiménez Ortega — Physics student (UGR) Jaén.

item.dc:creator: Miguel Jiménez Ortega

item.content:encoded:
Reading time: 9 minutes

Meitner is one of the least valued women in the history of physics, and we could say of humanity in general. She was a key person for the discovery and development of nuclear fission, although history was not entirely fair to her; today my colleague Laura and I bring you the marvellous story of this woman who leaves no one indifferent.

Early years. Childhood and arrival at university.

Lise Meitner was born in Vienna in 1878 into a Jewish family. Her father, Philipp Meitner, was a lawyer. Lise was the third of 8 siblings and all grew up in an intellectual environment encouraged by her father, a humanist who organised numerous gatherings in his house with prominent personalities.

At only 8 years old, Lise already showed signs of the curiosity that science awoke in her, especially mathematics (her grandmother told the anecdote that she slept with a mathematics book under her pillow). However, although she finished school with good grades, women could not go to university according to Austrian law. Public schooling ended at 14 years of age for women.

In 1897 the Austrian government decided to grant women access to the faculties of philosophy and medicine. Both Lise and her sister Gisela took advantage of this opportunity and were 2 of the 4 young women who passed the university entrance exam.

Lise entered the University of Vienna in Mathematics and Physics in October 1901. In her second year of university, all the subjects in which she enrolled were taught by the same professor: the theoretical physicist Ludwig Boltzmann. This professor fascinated Lise with his dedication to teaching and his treatment of his students. She remembered him thus:

[He] may have felt hurt by many things that another, stronger person would hardly have noticed. […] I believe that he was such a powerful teacher only because of his uncommon humanity.

Lise Meitner. A life in Physics. Ruth Lewin Sime

She finished her degree in 1905 and began her doctorate in a project directed by Franz Exner. Her doctoral thesis, “Conduction of Heat in Non-homogeneous Solids”, obtained the grade of summa cum laude under the supervision of Exner and Boltzmann. In spite of having obtained a doctorate, she had very few possibilities of working as a scientist.

Boltzmann’s death (in 1906) was decisive in Lise’s life. She promised herself not to abandon physics in spite of the obstacles. She spoke of him as:

He was in some way ‘a pure soul’, full of goodness, idealism and reverence for the wonder of the natural order of things.

Lise Meitner. A life in Physics. Ruth Lewin Sime

Fighting against the era.

In 1907, Lise Meitner arrived in Berlin. Meitner then met the one who would be her great work colleague for many years, the chemist Otto Hahn, in September of that same year, and she decided to work with him. But not everything was so easy for her. Emil Fisher, director of the KWIC institute (Kaiser Wilhelm Institut für Chemie) where Hahn worked, did not let women enter. In the end Meitner had to work in a room in the basement of the institute. But this did not stop her, and the Hahn–Meitner pair soon showed signs of their great research potential: by the end of 1908 they had already published several articles of great importance in their respective fields.

Figure: Photo of Lise Meitner and Otto Hahn in the laboratory. For almost 30 years they worked jointly and formed a superb working pair.

Meitner’s great capacity became noticeable over the years. In 1917 she is named section director of the KWIC and a year later she is named university professor. Her fame was such that during the 1930s she managed to join the ranks of physics as an honorary man. This title was shared only by Marie Curie and her daughter Irène. In October 1933 she participates in the Solvay conference together with great eminences of the physics of those years.

Figure: Solvay conference held in Brussels in October 1933. As the photo caption indicates, Meitner is second from the right. The two women who are seen on the left are, from left to right, Irène Joliot-Curie and Marie Curie respectively.

Flight from Nazi Germany.

In spite of being a recognised scientist, this was not enough for her to beat the antisemitism of the National Socialists. Her Jewish roots did not leave Hitler’s regime indifferent, and with the passing of the years during the decade of 1930 her situation became more complicated. In 1933 she was dismissed from her post at the University of Berlin and there was practically an attempt to remove and isolate her from the German scientific scene. Even so, Meitner was accustomed to fighting against all odds and managed to continue having an active role in research until 1938. That year, Hahn, due to internal pressures, found himself forced to dismiss her from the institute of chemistry after twenty years of joint work with her.

From here, the situation worsened; seeing the situation, professional colleagues with whom she had struck up friendship tried to offer her escape routes from Germany. Paul Scherrer invited her to give a talk in Zurich and Bohr did the same from Copenhagen. Although she was slow to accept because she resisted seeing the real situation in which she found herself. When at last she decided to go to Copenhagen, her visa for Denmark was denied to her. With this background, her colleagues soon set to work against the clock to get her out of the country. Dirk Coster, an old friend of hers, received confirmation on July 11 that she would be admitted into Holland. On the 13th, Coster and Meitner crossed the border without further incident.

It is interesting to mention how Meitner herself described this event and the high tension that she lived through, even reaching a nervous breakdown. She said:

At the Dutch border I got the fright of my life when a Nazi military patrol of five men who were checking the carriages collected my Austrian passport. I knew that the Nazis had just declared the hunting season open against the Jews. For ten minutes I remained seated waiting, which seemed to me as many hours. Then one of the Nazi officials returned and gave me back my passport without saying anything more.

The making of the Atom Bomb. Rhodes, R., Simon & Schuster, New York, 1986. p. 236

Legacy and injustice in history.

Focusing on the more technical aspect of her contribution to science, Meitner is a woman who contributed to a great extent over the years. In the first years and during most of her work in Germany she focused on nuclear chemistry and was especially interested in Uranium, above all in the decade of the 30s. In 1907 she published a study on the interaction of alpha particles in Physikalische Zeitschrift, where she explained that the scattering of these particles increased with atomic mass. This discovery would lead Rutherford to formulate the model of the atomic nucleus.

In 1914, during the First World War, Lise collaborated as an X-ray technician in a hospital at the same time as she researched uranium. In 1917 she created the Meitner Laboratory, and in 1918 she discovered a new element together with Otto Hahn: protactinium (Pa).

But without doubt the period of greatest contribution was from 1930 on. With the discovery of the neutron scientists launched themselves into searching for elements heavier than Uranium, and into seeing the different processes in which new elements or isotopes were created. Hahn and Meitner focused on the latter. When Meitner had to flee Germany, in 1938, everything was cut short; Hahn and his assistant did not deeply understand the processes in which Uranium split into other elements. Hahn wrote numerous letters to Lise with his doubts, and she never had any qualms about answering them. It was in these exchanges of correspondence that the idea of nuclear fission began to be forged, which brought atomic energy with it.

Without doubt the last part is among the most interesting and transcendent. The theoretical modelling of the fission of Uranium was carried out by Meitner and her nephew Otto Fischer. Hahn, however, did not include her as co-author in the publication, and both were deprived of the Nobel in Chemistry, which Hahn would win alone in 1944.

Conclusion to a scientist without palliatives.

In the following years Meitner continued with admirable scientific work; she was proposed to work on the Manhattan project, but she declined it because she did not want to see herself involved in the creation of a bomb. Lise Meitner is a clear example of the great impact that women have had on science in spite of always fighting against the current. Finally, she would die in Cambridge, on October 27, 1968, leaving a legacy that keeps resonating today, but that without doubt needs to be remembered.

item.title: Reality as we "know" it. What is out there?
item.dc:creator: Miguel Jiménez Ortega
item.description: Reading time: 7 minutes Today I bring you one of those topics that leave you thinking for weeks and that are never forgotten. What problems does science face nowadays? Is there a base problem in the vision that science has of the world? What place does the mind occupy in this…
item.content:encoded:
Reading time: 7 minutes

Today I bring you one of those topics that leave you thinking for weeks and that are never forgotten. What problems does science face nowadays? Is there a base problem in the vision that science has of the world? What place does the mind occupy in this construction of reality?

Subject–object relation. The problem of the ice cube.

After so many years of scientific research we have managed to elaborate models of a large part of the “reality” that we have around us. But, have you, the reader, ever had the audacity to ask yourself what the step is between what we observe and measure and what we experience, in terms of sensory perception, ourselves in our body?

Let us give an example: from a very young age we have widely distinguished (at the expense of an inevitable personal cost) between the concepts of cold and of heat. If they asked us about different objects we could immediately link them to whether they would produce in us one thing or the other. On the other hand, we have in our mind a tendency to establish an intrinsic relation (or so we believe; we will see whether this is so clear) between this sensation of “heat” and “cold” and the temperature at which the object in question is found.

Now, however, I propose to the reader that they imagine an ice cube. It is clear that if they asked you what type of sensation touching it would produce in you, you would answer quickly that cold. Obvious, it seems: ice is nothing more than water in a state of aggregation that is produced below 0ºC, and it is clear that this temperature, even without touching the ice, would already anticipate for us the answer to what is posed to us. But if you thought more carefully, you would realise, from personal experience, that if you touched an ice cube for a somewhat longer period of time, inevitably you would have to stop touching it, since you would feel “that it burns”. What has happened? Is the idea of cold and of heat no longer so clear?

Uncomfortable questions. Apparent reality.

What has occurred in the previous paragraph, expounded in a simple example from everyday life, can be summarised in one sentence: We have no idea how our senses and our brain make us perceive what we feel every day. This is without doubt a statement that is, at the very least, uncomfortable and at first sight perhaps too ambitious, but let us go further.

Erwin Schrödinger, a physicist widely recognised on the scientific scene, was also interested in these topics; in his essay Mind and Matter he talks about this problem that we tackle here, concretely in his last chapter titled The mystery of the sensual qualities. He poses uncomfortable questions for us and even for physics itself. In a concrete paragraph on page 115, he poses, with regard to light as a physical entity and the perception that we have of it:

The objective physical image of the wavelengths does not account for the sensation of colour. Could a physiologist do so if he had a better knowledge of what occurs in the retina and in the nervous system (…)? I do not believe so. We would attain, at most, which optical fibres are stimulated in particular; perhaps we would even come to know the processes that are produced in certain nerve cells (…). But not even this knowledge would tell us the slightest thing about the sensation of colour.

Mind and Matter. E. Schrödinger. Tusquets Editores, Metatemas.

What can be extracted from all this is that Schrödinger posed the question that we know, in our theoretical models, that for example yellow light is an electromagnetic wave which, if it is monochromatic, is found with a value of its wavelength of 589 nm. These are properties deduced from our models, but there is nothing in the concept of “wavelength” that tells me the slightest thing about the yellow colour that I experience. What is more, this same colour I could perceive equally if I mix other different colours (with different wavelengths) and I could say little about the relation between the physical idea that I have in mind and what I perceive.

The key to the problem. Objective reality.

If the reader has been brave enough to reach this point of the article, it is fair that they be recognised the merit of not having run away halfway through it. Without doubt the most exciting part remains, but also what will make our head finally end up exploding. Schrödinger summarises in his essay in a quite eloquent way what is discussed in what follows:

The direct sensory perception of the phenomenon says nothing of its objective physical nature (…) and must be disconnected from the beginning as a source of information, but the theoretical image that we eventually obtain always consists of a set of complicated pieces of information obtained through sensory perception.

Mind and Matter. E. Schrödinger. Tusquets Editores, Metatemas.

Schrödinger gives us the key to the problem: there is an abyss between what we “see” and what “really is”. The base of our knowledge is founded (only) on what our senses in the last instance show us of the world, but this tells us nothing of what we really have in front of us. A glass is a glass, as far as what we perceive of it, what our eyes and hands detect of it, but they do not capture its total reality; let us imagine that the glass were made of a material that emits in infrared or ultraviolet: we could say little about the total reality of the light that the glass emits if we did not make a more exhaustive study.

The always unsatisfactory answer.

Based on what has been expounded in the previous chapter, we should deny as a source of information the partial image that the senses show us. This is what we try, in effect, when we elaborate the theoretical model, a model “outside all sensory perception” supported by an “objective” science such as mathematics; but it turns out that we have arrived at this “model” precisely through diverse sensory experiences (experiments), that is, at the beginning of the process of knowledge we use our senses, in order, in the final process of elaborating the model, to eliminate them radically.

The question, then, we answer with other questions: Is our image of the universe a partial and incomplete vision? Can we really know the objective reality of the object? Only time will give us the answer. In case anyone curious wanted to go deeper into the topic, the following video is highly recommendable: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zV43vOXErKM&t=920s — Quite an interesting video created by Javier Santaolalla and Enric Fernández.

Author’s note: after a (rather philosophical) review of the present article I have been given the criticism that perhaps my approach is rather Platonic and even Kantian; I am guilty, perhaps, of my undeniable relation to the way of working and of thinking in my degree, physics. Therefore, if there is among the readers some philosopher more experienced in the topic, I am open to their making any comment that they consider opportune; likewise I leave in the bibliography some links/books where everything that I have expounded is explained much better.

Acknowledgements: thanks to my friend Manolo, much more experienced than I in philosophy, for the corrections and advice.

Bibliography

  • Mind and Matter. E. Schrödinger, Tusquets Editores. Metatemas.
  • For a much deeper reading, read Man on his Nature (Hombre versus Naturaleza), Sir Charles Sherrington.

  • For a vision of the problems of quantum mechanics from a philosophical point of view: https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/qt-issues/

Miguel Jiménez Ortega. Physics student (UGR).

item.title: The physics that is not seen: Learning on holiday. #2
item.dc:creator: Miguel Jiménez Ortega
item.description: Reading time: 6 minutes In this second instalment about the physics of the marvellous world that surrounds us day by day we go from the curiosities of our own satellite to the magic given off by those insects that are capable of walking on top of the water; we hope that you…
item.content:encoded:
Reading time: 6 minutes

In this second instalment about the physics of the marvellous world that surrounds us day by day we go from the curiosities of our own satellite to the magic given off by those insects that are capable of walking on top of the water; we hope that you enjoy it and, as always, that you take away a little knowledge about everything that happens around you.

What the moon hides from us.

Has the reader ever heard talk of the hidden face of the moon, and wondered why that face remains “hidden”? What is it afraid of? Today at Quantum Society we come to give the answer to that interesting question.

In reality the moon is not afraid of anything, nor does it have to do with any flat-earther physical theory. In reality this is a natural phenomenon, which is called synchronous rotation or tidal locking, and in reality it is quite a lot more common than it might seem. What happens is that the Moon (in our case) has the same period of rotation as of translation; said another way: it takes it the same time to go once around the Earth as to turn once on itself.

Figure: The Moon passes through diverse phases, but always shows us the same face.

This means that it takes almost 30 days to rotate and translate (27.32 days to rotate, and 29.53 days to translate). This is mainly because our satellite (like most of those of the solar system) has a non-uniform mass; therefore the gravitational attraction of the Earth on the Moon is always more intense on one part of it than on the other, generating a torque on it, which makes this “coupling” in its movement occur; so to speak, gravity always forces our satellite to show the same face, due to this non-uniformity in the distribution of its mass.

Tears of a saint.

As it could not be otherwise, we could not let escape the marvellous opportunity of showing our reader the origin and the reason for what in Spain is commonly known as Tears of Saint Lawrence or Perseids, for the more rigorous.

Without doubt we are talking about the most popular meteor shower of the year, and which occurs between the months of July–August. Its physical origin in itself is simple: all of them are nothing more than minuscule fragments that come from the comet 109P/Swift-Tuttle, which orbits the Sun with an approximate period of 133 years. The name Perseids comes to them because, looking at the starry sky with the naked eye, it seems that they come from the constellation of Perseus, although as we have already explained they have little to do with it. The luminous effect that we observe is due to the contact of these fragments with our atmosphere, which makes them volatilise and leave this so characteristic halo.

Figure: Night of Perseids in the Sky seen from Gran Canaria.

It is curious to mention that this same comet from which the Perseids come is one of those that have been catalogued as “dangerous objects” within our solar system; due to its own orbit, it has a certain probability of collision with the Earth (although in reality this is quite small) for the year 4479. Yes, we can breathe easy, but our great-great-great-great-great-great-great-grandchildren may perhaps get a fright. (Forgive me, reader, if I have overdone the “greats”; I wanted to give a certain emphasis to the moment).

The walking wizard of physics.

Has the reader ever seen one of those insects, walkers on water? Authentic wizards, but their trick in reality does not have so much of magic; it is pure physics: concretely, it takes advantage of a characteristic of fluids: surface tension.

The pond skater (Gerris lacustris) is the most common of these walkers. We can see it in lakes or places where the water does not present much movement. The lack of movement is an important factor so that this “boat” does not sink, because when the water is in a turbulent regime (as in a waterfall, or some river rapids) the cohesion forces between the molecules would no longer affect a large surface such as a lake, but rather smaller portions of water; that is why we usually see these insects in calm waters.

It is because of this characteristic of fluids that on many occasions we hurt ourselves when we throw ourselves into the swimming pool in a “not very hydrodynamic” way (a belly flop, as it has always been called). Surely the reader will have noticed that in high-altitude dives they spray with a jet of water at high velocity the zone where the diver is going to make their entry into the water, so that it breaks the surface tension and thus the spectacular pirouette does not end in any incident.

In conclusion: surface tension is the force that holds together the molecules of the water surface, and keeps the pond skaters afloat. It is also to blame for the pain that we feel when we throw ourselves into the water parallel to the horizon.

For the curious mathematicians.

As was already done in the previous chapter, for those who feel a certain motivation for how all these curiosities are posed from a more rigorous and formal point of view, with mathematics applied to physics, here are left some interesting expressions:

Celestial dynamics:

For all the astronomy part that we have seen today, we can extract as an interesting part how certain properties of the trajectories and of the orbits of the objects of the solar system can be calculated in the first instance. In principle the intention was to expound all the equations, but in this way this section becomes excessively long for us, which is not what is intended; therefore two links are shown where they are expounded. Many problems can be posed from classical mechanics with the Laws of Kepler and those of Newton. These are a set of laws among the most important in classical physics.

Surface tension:

In this section we cannot tackle great mathematical formulas either, since surface tension is more a concept than a mathematical development. We could say that the force that holds up the insect in this case is the result of a set of intermolecular forces that make an effective force arise that compensates the weight of the animal itself.

item.title: Chandrasekhar, the father of black holes.
item.dc:creator: Miguel Jiménez Ortega
item.description: Reading time: 8 minutes Last August 21, 25 years passed since the death of Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar, one of the great scientists of the 20th century. His contribution to the knowledge of the stars and the evolution of these was key to understanding some processes of the…
item.content:encoded:
Reading time: 8 minutes

Last August 21, 25 years passed since the death of Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar, one of the great scientists of the 20th century. His contribution to the knowledge of the stars and the evolution of these was key to understanding some processes of the universe. Today I bring you the life of this great man within the biographies section on our website.

Early years, childhood, university and arrival in Cambridge.

On October 19, 1910 was born in Lahore, which now belongs to the current Republic of Pakistan, one of the great physicists of the modern age, Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar. His father, Chandrasekhara Subrahmanya Ayyar, was a civil servant who worked in the Indian government. His mother, Sita (neé Balakrishnan), a translator by profession, was a person of great intelligence. He himself describes her as a person deeply dedicated to her children. During his first years he received a great education on account of his parents. In 1918 the family moved to Madras (currently the city of Chennai), where it settled in the following years.

Figure: S. Chandrasekhar with his 4 brothers and 6 sisters in Madras, India. From left to right, seated: Bala, Savitri, Chandra, Sarada, Rajam; above: Vidya, Balakrishnan, Vishwam, Ramanathan, Sundari.

In Madras he went to the Hindu high school, in the year 1922. Three years later, in 1925, he began his university stage at the Presidency College. Chandra, as those closest to him used to call him, already showed during his stay at the university a certain capacity to solve problems. At 18 years of age, he began to write his first scientific works. In June 1930 he finished his degree in Physics. Months later he received from the Indian government a scholarship to study in Cambridge.

During these years of university stage he would also meet the one who would be the love of his life, Lalitha Doraiswamy. With her he married years later, in September 1936. In his autobiography on the Nobel prize page, referenced in the notes, he spoke of his wife in the following way:

During the 47 years that we shared of our lives, Lalitha’s patient understanding, support and courage were the central parts of my life.

Subramanyan Chandrasekhar – Facts. NobelPrize.org. Nobel Media AB 2020. Mon. 24 Aug 2020.

Figure: Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar and Lalitha Doraiswamy Chandrasekhar at the ceremony dedicated to the McDonald observatory in 1939. (Photograph property of Elwood M. Payne, UChicago Photographic Archive, apf1-01661, University of Chicago Library)

Postgraduate studies, beginning of his scientific career.

Upon his arrival in Cambridge, he became a research student under the supervision of professor R.H Fowler. He finished the doctorate in 1933. During this year he also forged a friendship with Arthur Eddington. Eddington was one of the historical figures who motivated him to establish the model of stellar evolution that would bear his name, the Chandrasekhar model.

It is said that during the journey of arrival to Cambridge, he read the book The Internal Constitution of the Stars, by Eddington himself. In it, Arthur defended that the death of all stars had the same end: they ended up forming into what is called a white dwarf. Chandra demonstrated that this end depends on the star’s own mass and that only for some is this destiny fulfilled. However, others, where the mass is greater than the Chandrasekhar limit, can end up collapsing into a black hole or, even, end up in a supernova.

In the year 1935, he had a slight setback in his academic life. During a talk at the Royal Astronomical Society, he and Eddington argued about the two visions that they had regarding stellar evolution. During the winter of 1936 they offered him a position at the University of Chicago (United States) as associate professor. He would enter there in 1937 and it is where he would remain for the rest of his academic life.

Figure: Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar at the University of Chicago. Some say that the argument with Eddington was one of the circumstances that pushed him to lean towards the United States.

Academic stage. The super professor of Chicago.

After having studied at one of the best universities in the world, Chandra began his new stage in Chicago. Lalitha, in the emotive chapter My Everlasting Flame of the book Chandrasekhar: The Man Behind the Legend – Chandra Remembered talks about the last days of life of Subrahmanyan and about the whole of his life. In it she describes how he began his first years as a professor of the university. She highlights that for her husband teaching had been a great discovery since this facet helped him to better understand what he himself had studied or was studying. She mentions in the book:

He developed a great amount of teaching, often oriented to his own research, since he firmly felt that this was the best way to clarify his thoughts with respect to what he was researching.

Chandrasekhar: The Man Behind the Legend – Chandra Remembered

His intellectual capacity left no one indifferent, well known was the admiration that his university students professed for him and the capacity that he had to make the desire to learn awaken in them. Bimla Buti, a student who met Subramanyan during a course on quantum mechanics that he taught in Chicago, spoke thus about him from her deep respect:

He was a super professor. All of us used to be spellbound (in his classes). (…) For any specific problem that he chose, he investigated all its possible aspects with complete mathematical rigor and in depth. This is exactly what for a long time made him publish a great variety of articles on different topics.

Chandrasekhar: The Man Behind the Legend – Chandra Remembered

There he spent all his life; nowadays he is remembered in the American city as one of the great eminences of the university and a figure with an unprecedented historical repercussion.

Scientific legacy: works and contributions to humanity.

Subrahmanyan’s way of working was quite remarkable. As he himself explains, his methodology was the following: he first sought to find a part of physics that he saw could be cultivated, he took pains to go deep into that field and, once he considered and saw himself with sufficient knowledge, he contributed his point of view. This is how he managed to work on and publish different articles in a great variety of topics within physics.

He himself highlighted seven stages in his life referring to the topic to which he dedicated himself: in the first he worked on stellar evolution, where he includes his work on white dwarfs (1929-1939), the second deals with stellar dynamics, including Brownian motion (1938-1943), the third covers the theory of radiative transfer (1943-1950), the fourth is about hydrodynamics and hydromagnetic stability (1952-1961), in the fifth he got involved in the equilibrium and the stability of ellipsoidal figures of equilibrium (1961-1968), during the sixth he already relaxed a little and worked on the general theory of relativity (1962-1971) and for the seventh and last he ended up working on the mathematical theory of black holes (1974-1983).

As we can verify, the work and the capacity of this man were impressive. During the Second World War he worked on the Manhattan Project. He stood out in different topics, but without doubt his most important contribution was his works referring to stellar evolution and structure, for which he would receive the Nobel in 1983 shared with his tutor R.H Fowler. In 1999 NASA named one of its great observatories the Chandra X-ray Observatory; there even exists an asteroid that bears his name, 1958 Chandra.

Introduction.

A couple of weeks ago we launched on the website the exciting biography of Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar. A figure who left no one indifferent. We were talking about how, among his many contributions to physics, one of the most interesting was to establish a theoretical model in which he explained that not all stars would end up forming into white dwarfs and that there would be a limiting mass that would define this. If the critical mass was greater than the one Chandra postulated, a black hole could form due to the collapse of the star. Today we are going to try to explain this in the most intuitive and didactic way possible.

In what follows we are going to use terminology and concepts of statistical physics, quantum physics and thermodynamics, among others. Although it is a research article (as we classify it on the website), I am going to try nonetheless that it can be followed by the greatest number of people possible, so do not get scared if your knowledge is not very advanced; simply enjoy the beauty of the mathematics and the physics that I show you now.

Basic concepts of statistical physics.

Before getting fully into the whole formulation of the problem, we are going to talk briefly about some concepts of statistical physics. As its own name indicates, in this branch of physics we use statistics to obtain general properties of those systems whose components are enormously large (a gas, for example, whose number of molecules can resemble values such as that of Avogadro’s number). To describe the systems we use what are called ensembles, which are nothing more than functions that describe the probability that a microstate resolves into a given macrostate.

Since surely you are asking yourself, I am going to answer you about what a macrostate is and what a microstate is, but I am going to give you an example, which I believe is how things are best understood. Imagine a box where there are lots of balls. All move from one side to another with a different velocity and constantly changing their position, as in Figure 1. Well, a microstate would be as if we took and snapped a photo of the system at a determined moment. In that photo all the balls would have a fixed position and velocity. That is, a microstate is one of the possible states in which each and every one of the (microscopic) components that form the system can be.

Figure 1. Exemplification of a box full of balls moving continuously.

The macrostate also describes properties of the system, but as its name indicates, it accounts for macroscopic properties, such as for example temperature, pressure, etc., which moreover are variables measurable in a laboratory. For different systems there exists a certain probability that a microstate gives the complete system some concrete values of temperature, energy, pressure… A macrostate can never define the microstate, but the inverse option will indeed occur. To finish this summary (very summarised and much summary) we are going to talk about partition functions. The only thing that interests us is that these functions act as the constant that normalises the ensemble, that is, the number by which one divides so that everything is normalised to one, since probability can only be between 0 and 1. The only thing that interests us is that these functions are related to the thermodynamic potentials, which again are functions that describe the thermodynamic properties of the systems. If you have studied some bachillerato (high school), you have already worked with two without knowing it: internal energy and entropy itself!

Grand canonical ensemble, partition function and grand canonical potential.

After this brief introduction, we now begin with the formulas. All those that are going to appear have their formal deduction, but we will skip some steps since it is not a matter of boring everyone. Chandra uses for his model one of the partition functions that we have just talked about, the grand canonical partition function; this we use to describe those systems that allow an exchange of energy and of particles with the exterior. In the example of our box we would use this partition function if, for example, there were a flow of balls from our box to another connected with it.

The expression of this function, within the very quantum formalism of the theory, presents this aspect.

(†)

Equation 1

A priori it is not excessively complicated; it is a product over the quantum numbers k of the particles (which in this case are fermions, like the electron, but if you want we can talk about that another day) of one plus an exponential raised to some factors that we are not going to describe in excess either. and (†) are two factors linked to the temperature and the flow of particles of the system respectively; we simply must keep that in mind for now.

Up to here, all the more or less introductory part. One must take into account that we are working with much more subtle concepts, and it is normal that we are skipping some steps and that the reader often asks where things come from. Everything is deduced, and we will try to ensure that this feeling is not had in a generalised way during the reading of the article.

Chandrasekhar’s approach.

Chandra pictures a white dwarf as a gas of fermions that is completely degenerate and, watch out, they are relativistic. Of course he has his arguments, but we will not go into more detail. He also works in what is called the thermodynamic limit (for our vocabulary it would be when everything becomes very large). Due to this, all the summations that appear make a jump to the continuum and become integrals. Now yes, let’s go for the equations!

The first thing that we must keep in mind is where we want to arrive. Let us remember that we want to establish a limiting mass by which the dying star turns into a white dwarf or into something else (a black hole for example); therefore I am going to arrive at an equation where I will equate the two forces that act on the star, that of the internal pressure and that of gravity. Here, I will ask myself about its radius and the relation with its mass, since this will tell me if there is some limit for it to collapse or not (to collapse, its radius would have to become zero). We are going to look for the expression of the pressure; the interesting part begins!

With all this in our heads, let’s put on our work overalls and get our hands dirty; I assure you that the result will not disappoint you. The first thing that we do to obtain the expression of the pressure is to use a thermodynamic potential, the grand canonical potential, which is defined as appears in Equation (2):

Here a summation appears because we have to remember that the logarithm of a product is equal to the sum of logarithms. This is one of the best-known properties of logarithms. Once the sum is expounded, we are going to make the mentioned jump to the continuum. Our grand canonical potential would remain as in Equation (3).

Equation 3

Surely you will be asking yourself where some terms have come from; we will comment on them briefly. The g is called the degeneracy parameter; we simply have to keep in mind that for the electron it is 2, which is why in the next equations an 8 (4×2) will appear. We must also mention the h; this is nothing more than Planck’s constant, and it serves simply so that the units match, so for us it does not have much meaning either, but it is good to comment on it. The main idea that you have to keep is that they are terms that appear to compensate the fact that we have substituted the summation by the integral. In the appendix I have written how the expression of the last integral of Equation (3) is obtained; don’t worry, nothing slips past us here.

Although it does not seem so, we have already managed to obtain the expression for the pressure. The grand canonical potential, by definition in thermodynamics, can also be written as the product of the pressure by the volume. So if we equate the expression of the potential to (†) we will be able to solve for the pressure, which in this case is very simple since the (†) goes away by being on one side and the other of the equation. In this way we arrive at Equation (4).

(For the mathematically curious, surely if I say “un día vi una vaca vestida de uniforme” [“one day I saw a cow dressed in uniform”, the Spanish mnemonic for ], it will sound more familiar to them). We also have our reasons for taking this limit; I will try to close it all a bit more in the final notes. Now we are going to put the expression explicitly; remember that Chandrasekhar supposed relativistic fermions, therefore the expression that we must use is (†). Development of the theory. (3)

Finally we arrive at the last section of the theory; if you have held out until here, at the very least you deserve a master’s in physics. But well, let’s go for the important part, to see what the death of the star holds in store for us.

The step that we are going to carry out now is the last in order to be able to solve the integral, although we will not solve it explicitly, since in the end we will have to make an approximation in a certain limit, the relativistic one. Therefore we pose a change of variable inside the integral, of the form (†). When we carry out the change, an expression like Equation (10) remains.

This integral can be solved analytically (with pencil and paper), and I encourage the reader who wants to, to solve it with the techniques that they know; we have already done the integral and have put it as the expression of a function, A(x), where our variable x is (†) and where, after a series of calculations that do not fit in this brief exposition, one arrives at the fact that there exists a dependence between x and the radius of the star of the form 1/R. Finally the last expression, the one we were looking for, for the pressure is:

Do you remember that we said that at the very end we would equate the two forces that intervened? Well, the moment has arrived; this is shown in Equation (12), where we have equated the force exerted by the internal pressure (remember that force is pressure times surface and (†) is the surface of a sphere, which we liken to the star) and the gravitational one.

Conclusion.

The only thing that remains to do is to substitute the pressure that appears in Equation (12) by the expression that we have obtained; from here we will obtain a relation between the radius and the mass. It is a somewhat tedious calculation, but the dependence itself is not complicated to get out if one puts some effort into it. Finally the relation between the radius and the mass is:

Equation 13

The approximation that we were talking about before is that A(x) in the relativistic case has the form of (†); this expression is the one we use to arrive at Equation (13). As we see, an (†) appears in the formula. This is the critical mass that Chandrasekhar found and that demonstrated that not all stars would end their life, under these conditions, transformed into a white dwarf. For those that have a greater mass, their gravitational force will overcome the internal pressure and the star will finally collapse into a black hole. If the calculation is done explicitly, this critical mass has a value of 1.44 solar masses.

The key of the calculation was above all to take into account the relativistic effects in the physical system. Fowler, also a physicist, did the same calculation a few years before but without taking into account this factor; in the end he obtained an expression where there was no critical mass that defined the future of the system.

Appendix.

Due to the great level of compression of the knowledge, there have been some parts of the exposition where some steps have been skipped; we are going to comment on them below:

  • Firstly, I suppose that the reader will have been confused as to why I have changed the k for the p in some expressions without hardly mentioning it; this derives from the study of a quantum system in an isolated system such as a box. There exists a relation between the momentum p of the particles and the quantum number k to describe their wave function.
  • I also suppose that the reader will have asked themselves why one nonetheless arrives at an integral where the limits are 0 and a certain (†). This is because fermions at low temperatures are distributed in such a way that each one is found at a different energy level, staggered and occupying them all, and they form what is called a sea of fermions. In this case not all the energy levels of the system are occupied, but rather there exists a limit where the last fermion that remains is placed; the energy that this last fermion occupies is called the Fermi energy, which incidentally is related to the Fermi pressure, (†). This is why the integral is only done over that stretch, not over all the levels. The other thing that may sound strange is that there is a factor of the integral that disappears completely; this is because the expression (†) is exactly the expression for the mean occupation of an energy level for fermions, which in the case of low temperatures is 1 for all those that are below the Fermi energy and 0 for those that are above (since there are none; the one that is at the Fermi energy is the last one).
  • One might ask why in the last steps we have taken a limit with the temperature at almost 0 K. The point is that what interests us is not so much the temperature itself, but the energy scale in comparison with the already-mentioned Fermi energy. Since one is much greater than the other, the system behaves the same as in the limit of temperatures close to 0.
  • Another important aspect that we must mention is how, in Equation (3), we pass from one integral to the other. Initially we have a vector integral over phase space. One has to realise that what is inside the integral, the integrand, only depends on the modulus of the momentum p of the particle (remember that q and p are vectors; they have components , and (†), for example in Cartesians, and they also have a modulus). Therefore the integral in the vector dq we can do, since our integral separates (I know that some mathematicians are hating me right now). And what then is integrating over all the positions of all the particles in phase space in a continuum? Effectively, the total volume. On the other hand, for the vector dp, we use a type of coordinates called spherical (I know, perhaps if your level is not very advanced you have never heard of them, but don’t worry) to easily carry out the integral. These are distributed into the angular part and a radial part, which is the one that has to do with the modulus of the vector; therefore all the angular part, as there is no dependence at all, remains as a constant and only the integral in dp (modulus) remains for us. In the integration by parts, on differentiating the (†) there appeared a (†) which went away with the (†) that we had outside. Another comment about the nuances of the integrals: in some expressions I have not put the limits of integration, but simply for an aesthetic reason. All the integrals are definite integrals, not indefinite.
  • As a last comment, I will stop to explain why we equate the two forces mentioned before to draw conclusions. The idea is that just when these two forces are equal, nothing would happen to the star; it would remain in equilibrium. In this situation, if we look for the relation between the different variables, we can determine what happens if one increases or not and, based on this, know whether the equilibrium breaks towards one direction or another. The star can collapse or not.

Reading time: 6 minutes

Observing the world that surrounds us is always an exercise of inner humility that makes us realise how insignificant we are within the framework of the universe. During these chapters we have been talking about everything: quantum physics, particle physics, basic physics, applied physics… Today we bring you a new instalment where we try to explore another type of everyday experiences, but not at all boring ones.

Parking the car in the garage. A whole relativistic adventure.

Surely our dear reader has at some time had to find themselves in the dilemma of whether or not to park their automobile in the garage. The youngest may not have faced that problem yet, but we assure them that they will. Therefore let us imagine that one day we approach a company specialised in the construction of garages, where two people attend to us attentively: Galileo and Lorentz. The reader would inform them that their car measures 5 metres and that they would not like to spend much money on the purchase of the garage.

Galileo would without doubt offer that they buy a garage of 7 metres in length; in this way the car would have no problem getting in and there would be space to spare. However, our good Lorentz would recommend one of 4 metres, which is cheaper, and would assure us that our automobile would fit perfectly. Obviously this would surprise our reader, who would be left thinking for a good while and would curse themselves for wanting to buy a garage in such a grotesque place. What is the matter with Lorentz?

Galileo Galilei developed, among many other things, a way of transforming the coordinates of one reference system into another; these transformations are called Galilean, and of course they did not take into account relativistic factors.

Hendrik Antoon Lorentz was a recognised physicist of the past century and he also represents a set of coordinate transformations that also bear his name. Of course these do take into account relativistic factors and, for small velocities, they recover the form of those of Galileo.

Do not let the reader get frightened: obviously the car does not fit and will never fit in a garage smaller than it. What happens is that if our automobile were capable of entering the garage at a velocity close to that of light, for an observer who saw the movement from the pavement opposite, the car would indeed “enter” inside the garage for a brief time. This is because, from the point of view of the observer on the pavement, the car would undergo a Lorentz contraction. These phenomena are frequent when we work at velocities close to those of light. All this occurs because light, in any reference system that we take, has the same velocity, something “a priori” not very intuitive. This is one of the fundamental postulates of special relativity.

The physics of an indestructible glass.

Without any doubt at some moment of their life some of our readers have had the marvellous privilege of breaking a glass or a wine glass. We have all recognised that glorious moment in which, by pure chance, destiny chooses us to be the centre of attention for a time. Look, I told you so! or You’re just so hyper! are typical phrases that we have heard our mother say at that moment; ¡Alegría! [“Cheers!”] your uncle also sometimes hurries to shout. But without doubt there is something that could be going round the head of our dearest reader. Sometimes, glasses fall and do not break, or even other times, they shatter into pieces with a minimal touch. What magic is there in this strange behaviour?

The answer is ionic bonds. Without doubt some reader with a good memory will remember it from their stage in high school. This concept holds many more curiosities than it may seem. This type of bond between atoms is produced when we have two elements with a high difference in electronegativity, normally one metallic and another non-metallic. The curious thing is that due to their nature, the structures that form when many atoms coexist are called crystalline structures. These are the ones that give us the answers for this apparently strange behaviour.

Figure: Example of a crystal lattice for NaCl; it can be observed how in one colour the Cl atoms appear and in another those of Na.

The curious thing about these structures is that, looking at it in a simple way, the ions arrange themselves in a very orderly and quite rigid way. It is very complicated to deform them, and even if they fall they do not have to break. The problem comes when one manages precisely to give a blow that destabilises this order, since ions of equal sign repel each other very abruptly during a brief instant in which the lattice has been displaced, and an almost immediate breakage irremediably occurs. Even with a brief touch, if it is the right one, it is possible to see this effect.

For the most curious.

The explicit deduction, in a more or less easy way, of the Lorentz transformations is not excessively complicated and I encourage the brave ones who dare to take on this challenge; a trick to achieve it is: suppose two reference systems, one at rest and another at velocity v that only moves along one of the axes; from here propose a generic expression as a function of constants and take into account that the speed of light is the same in both. In any case, as is already given in the link, we have several posts written by Carlos where he develops a little more in depth all the aspects of special relativity.

For those who feel passionate about the types of bonds that exist, I encourage them to look for more information about them. At a simple level we highlight two more: the covalent and the metallic, with completely different properties. The physics that underlies these bonds is highly interesting; in quantum mechanics diverse methods are used to do mathematical calculations, such as perturbation theory. If you like what you read, ask for it in the comments and we will keep going deeper and deeper.

Reading time: 8 minutes

Translator’s note: four mathematical symbols of this article (the name of the triangle’s group, the Euclidean space, the identity matrix of expression (1) and the particle predicted by Gell-Mann) did not render in the source PDF. They have been reconstructed in standard notation and are marked with (†).

Today we bring one of the most surprising concepts when it comes to understanding and knowing how our universe works. Although everything seems to extend throughout it without an apparent order, physics and mathematics tell us that there is much more beyond what our perception barely dares to imagine. The symmetries that describe our systems will give us information about it even before we know of the existence of some of its components. Symmetries are used in special relativity, astrophysics or even in everyday physics. I encourage you to immerse yourself in this great adventure that knowing what the gearwork that moves the cosmos is constitutes.

Ordo ab chao. Symmetry in front of the mirror.

First day of the degree, first symmetry learned.

On the first day of faculty our first-year physics professor introduced us to the first class of the degree in the following way: “At first you will see physics as a jumble of disconnected and meaningless equations, you will not see correlation between any of them, and you will think that everything you study belongs to different parts of knowledge. But as you advance in your years of study you will see that more and more everything will be reduced to a set of fundamental laws and that the whole structure of the universe is summarised in a simple word: symmetries”.

The mirror as a physics teacher.

As well appears in Dan Brown’s novel “The Lost Symbol”, the expression ordo ab chao, order out of chaos, is what the knowledge of symmetries within our universe suggests to us. They are capable of putting order within the chaos that apparently reigns in it. But what is a symmetry? I suppose that the reader will have asked this question a few lines ago, but without doubt will not have realised that they see the answer every day in the mornings when they look in the mirror. Our reflection in the mirror is a type of symmetry; in this case it is called reflection and, although it is not exactly the same as the concept that we want to give, it serves us to understand it in first approximation.

First idea of the concept of symmetry.

To understand the concept completely with this idea of the mirror, we should imagine what would happen if, for example, I cut a starfish in half and stick it to the mirror by the cut side; obviously on looking at it from the front it would seem to me that the starfish is complete and has not suffered any type of cut. We have just found something fascinating: starfish contain a reflection symmetry with respect to the axis that cuts them in half. Translated into a mathematical language, the starfish remains intact on subjecting it to a reflection operation. These are the type of properties where the potential of symmetries resides, since they will help us to understand systems and extract information from them despite not working directly with them.

Group theory. From the simplest aspect to the most symmetric physics.

Concrete example: the triangle.

The mathematical theory that exists beneath all this vocabulary of symmetries is group theory. This theory works with the properties of systems and defines operations between the different transformations that they can undergo. Let us see a simple example but at the same time a very powerful one. Let us think of an equilateral triangle: how many transformations would the reader think they would be capable of doing to the triangle, without repeating them, that would leave it invariant? Let us see an example of a type of transformation that would fulfil these conditions. Let us think of a rotation of 120º. If the reader closed their eyes and I turned the triangle by this amount and afterwards they opened them again, would you notice any substantial difference from if, directly, I had done nothing to it? Indeed, you would see it exactly the same as at the beginning, as if nothing had changed.

Figure (1). The 120º rotation of an equilateral triangle leaves it invariant, as if we had done nothing. It also occurs with rotations of multiples of 120º such as 240º and 360º (this is the identity itself since rotating 360º is like rotating 0º, that is, not rotating at all). All these operations describe symmetries of this object. Image taken from: https://pixabay.com/es/vectors/geometr%C3%ADa-tri%C3%A1ngulos-curvo-forma-153158/

Doing it is not the same as seeming to do it.

It is important to differentiate before continuing between “as if we had done nothing” and “doing nothing”; in Figure (1) we see that if we assigned a number to each vertex of the triangle, on making changes we would indeed see that the labelled vertices have changed, but the global structure of the triangle has not; that is why it is not the same to talk about transformations that leave the triangle invariant, which seem as if we had done nothing to it, as to apply for example the identity transformation, which is literally making no change. In terms of numbers, it would be like multiplying a number by 1.

First complete example of a group.

It can be seen in a simple and curious exercise that there exist 6 types of transformations that leave the triangle invariant: three rotations of 120º, 240º and 360º (0º) and three reflections, with respect to each axis that passes through each vertex. All these operations form a discrete group, which we can call (†). All the operations between the elements of the group can be obtained explicitly and thus we will arrive at what is called the multiplication table of the group. For example, we can see that rotating the triangle twice is equivalent to doing a reflection about one of the axes.

Symmetries of SU(3), from the mathematical game to the physics of quarks.

From mathematics to physics.

The reader will ask what all this about triangles, reflections and rotations has to do with physics or with the world that surrounds us; patience, now is when it gets interesting. The key for working with groups is that they admit representations in vector spaces (do not be alarmed if you do not know what a vector space is; it is a mathematical construction to represent, for example, our real world of three dimensions), and these representations are given by matrices; the simplest example would be that of the identity transformation: how would it be represented in our Euclidean space (†)? Well, as it will surely sound familiar to you, in the form:

(†)

Ordering our space into symmetries.

We will not go into how the forms that the elements of the group will have in the space are found out; the important thing is that this is the way of working with them in physics. And now comes the most interesting part: following the structure of these groups, we can find vectors of the space where they are represented that remain invariant under the action of these elements of the group, yes, just as with the triangle. In this way we can separate our whole physical space into a set of subspaces formed by vectors that are invariant to some of the actions of the group. Perfect! We have just divided our space into a set of invariant parts (symmetries) described by the action of a group. This is the fundamental idea that resides in all this; this is how the hidden mechanism of the cosmos is broken down.

The best gift of the universe.

Therefore, what has all this served for? Is it really important? The answer is yes. During the second half of the last century, the scientist Gell-Mann suggested that the symmetry that was underneath the hadrons (that is what particles like the proton or neutron are called) was the one that underlies the group SU(3). Gell-Mann predicted the existence of particles that had not yet been found, such as the (†). He was even capable of telling experimental physicists how they should look for it and under which reaction it would be produced. The result? A few years later this particle was found and the power of the SU(3) symmetry was affirmed as the underlying symmetry beneath the particles that form hadrons: the quarks. Here is the marvellous picture that the universe gifts us.

  • S. Coleman, Aspects of Symmetry, Cambridge University Press, 1985.
  • W-K. Tung, Group Theory in Physics, World Scientific, 1985.

Reading time: 7 minutes

Introduction.

Welcome to one of the most fascinating theories that the human being has without doubt ever developed. Since this is the first chapter of this series I would like to make some comments before we enter into the grandiose world of cosmology, black holes, and all those phenomena that General Relativity describes.

I would like to highlight the academic aspect of these writings. Of course there will be concepts that at the mathematical level will be much more subtle and could be described in a much more formal way. But my idea is that these articles reach the greatest variety of public possible; it is therefore that an attempt will be made to find a balance between mathematical rigour and the qualitative discussion of the aspects that refer to this theory, trying not to fall, obviously, into boredom and excessive heaviness.

On the other hand, we have on the website a series dedicated to Special Relativity; for whoever may be interested it is highly recommendable.

Historical context, the problem of space and of time.

Relativity, a problem not at all simple.

Without doubt, throughout history the human being has had to face diverse problems; without going any further, see the case of this past year 2020. But among them, few have supposed an effort, at a mental level, as complex as was the development of General Relativity (from here on and in what follows we will denominate it GR). In the words of Einstein himself:

In my life I have never worked so hard: I have come to have a great respect for mathematics, whose more subtle parts I had until now naively considered as pure luxury. Compared with this problem, (special) relativity is child’s play.

Albert Einstein in a letter to A. Sommerfield. 1912.

Some philosophy in relativity.

And it is that it turned out to be a problem not only in the sense that the mathematics that it required were much more complex, but it also required a completely renewed vision of our conception of space and of time. But this story already came from afar; many other figures such as Leibniz, Newton, Clarke or Ernst Mach had already discussed at length about these questions. This last one is very little known but, nevertheless, he was among those who most influenced the thinking of the young Einstein. The two great blocks that confronted each other were the absolutists on one side and the relationists on the other. The key of the confrontation resided in studying the role of observers and of motion in nature. Do there exist universal, completely static reference systems with respect to which we could refer any motion?

Absolutism vs relationism. The bucket problem.

The eternal struggle.

Since Newton established his ideas of space and time in 1687, the eternal struggle between absolutism and relationism in the vision of the universe has never ceased. There is no room for doubt that it is a fascinating subject, but we will try to be precise so as not to bore our reader in excess. The key idea that Isaac Newton established was that of an absolute image of space and time, apart from the fact that he conceived them in an independent way, something quite interesting in the final idea that we will obtain with GR. But the counterpoint to this vision did not take long to arrive. The German philosopher Gottfried Leibniz had something to say. Leibniz did not agree with this posture. He argued that it was contradictory to affirm the existence of facts such as absolute location and velocity.

The definitive experiment.

This struggle continued with arguments for and against, and not only from philosophy but from physics itself; one of the most descriptive examples to which they tried to give an answer was the bucket experiment. This consisted of a thought experiment, which Newton and Samuel Clarke initially used to refute the arguments of Leibniz, where one imagined a bucket full of water spinning in the middle of the universe. Newton assured that in the spinning of the bucket the water showed a concave shape due to the rotation (something quite intuitive) but, what is more, the English scientist argued that this occurred because the water was accelerated with respect to a static reference system, preferred over all the others: absolute space. For Newton space exists as a real physical entity.

Two completely distant positions.

The truth is that Leibniz, however, did not think the same. The German philosopher believed that space did not exist in any conventional sense. It had no meaning in itself beyond simply providing the adequate language to locate the relative position of one object with respect to another. For Leibniz, a completely empty space would make as little sense as an alphabet that is missing its letters, since the alphabet provides an order for the 28 letters, but does not exist in itself independently of them. We find ourselves then with two opposed visions: Newton sees space as an entity where accelerated motion is not relative; on the other side we have Leibniz, who does not conceive space as an entity in itself and thinks that all aspects of motion are relative. At this point is when our already-mentioned Mach appears, who begins to shed light on all this muddy terrain of relationist and absolutist postures.

The universe of Mach. Influence on Einstein’s thinking.

Some light in the chaos.

After several years of philosophical discussion, our Austrian friend entered the scene. Although his position continues to accept several fundamental theses of relationism, Mach introduces a new approach when it comes to talking about relative motion and with respect to what we feel or do not feel that we are moving. The fact is that Mach still did not see space as a real physical entity, but his vision of accelerated motion changed subtly. For him, this was relative to the average mass distribution that was in the universe with respect to the observer in motion.

The key for Mach, an empty universe.

What Mach imagined is that there did not exist an intrinsic difference between moving or not moving (concretely between spinning or not spinning) in a space that was completely empty. What is more, he argued that in a universe where absolutely nothing existed it did not make sense even to ask about the concept of accelerated motion itself, since there were no reference systems with which to compare. Whether or not far from the veracity of this conception of space, what is undeniable is that Einstein was aware of Mach’s thinking and that it influenced him deeply in his first years of study.

Legacy of Mach, beginning of general relativity.

Einstein also thought that Newton’s vision was erroneous. The writings of Mach introduced him into the world of the relationist vision and gave him the opportunity to describe a universe that had no need at all of an absolute space as a preferred reference system. What is more, in his first steps towards GR, Einstein, in his description of special relativity, imagined a universe where space and time were individually relative. However and, although it may seem surprising, he conceived space-time as an absolute entity. Of course, this vision changed with the development of GR. From there on space and time began to be conceived as two faces of one same physical reality; thus began one of the greatest theories ever developed before by the human being.

Bibliography.

  • The Fabric of the Cosmos. Brian Green.
  • Notes on General Relativity (Apuntes de Relatividad General). Bert Janssen. University of Granada.
