Translator’s note: the mathematical symbols of this article did not render in the source PDF (they appear as blank spaces). The expressions shown here in LaTeX have been reconstructed in standard notation from the surrounding text.

A very old problem.

The old geometry of Euclid.

In the previous chapter we were talking about the different philosophical currents that had discussed the ideas of space and time. Today our battle consists in finding out how differential geometry arises, something extremely important for making a dynamic description of space-time. Our path begins with Euclid.

Euclidean geometry has been, during the greater part of our recent history, the one that has prevailed in all the aspects of the study of physical systems. It was not until the 19th century, when a young German mathematician called Georg Bernhard Riemann, that someone was able to imagine a geometry where not each and every one of Euclid’s postulates were fulfilled, and that moreover could be perfectly valid.

The fifth postulate.

It turns out that this problem had brought innumerable headaches to all mathematicians during the centuries after the publication of Euclid’s Elements. Euclidean geometry postulated that space was three-dimensional and that, moreover, it was flat. And this, my friends, was the postulate that most bothered the mathematical community:

Let it be postulated… That, if a straight line falling on two straight lines makes the interior angles on the same side less than two right angles, the two straight lines, if produced indefinitely, will meet on that side on which are the angles less than the two right angles.

Euclid. The Elements I, 32. 4th century B.C.

Translated into plain language we could say that this postulate comes to tell us something that intuitively we can observe ourselves if we take a sheet of paper and a pen: two parallel lines never cut each other, that is, they always keep between them a finite distance in the plane.

The possibility of imagining.

This postulate was the most difficult to interpret, since it was not known whether it was a theorem, provable with the rest of the four axioms, or was really a base principle from which one started, that is, an axiom like the other four. Gauss himself left it to his young student to explore the possibility of a geometry where the fifth postulate was not fulfilled. The humble and shy Riemann rose to the occasion. In a lecture given on June 10, 1854 at the University of Göttingen, Germany, Riemann surprised the world by opening a new field directed towards geometries of spaces with higher dimensions and, of course, not necessarily flat. It can be said that Riemann gave mathematicians the possibility of imagining spaces of more dimensions.

Basic concepts of curved geometry.

Concept of an N-dimensional manifold, .

One of the most important key concepts in this theory is that of a manifold. We know from special relativity that space-time at small scales, for example those of an experiment, must be Minkowski space, which is necessarily flat. With this intuitive idea of what we must look for, we now define what a manifold is: An N-dimensional manifold, , is an arbitrary space that locally, at small scales, resembles the N-dimensional flat space . At each point of the manifold one can define what is called the tangent space, , which is, in mathematical terms, isomorphic to .

Do not let the reader be frightened by this new terminology; just keep in mind that isomorphic means that they are practically equal. At a mathematical level the tangent space at each point and the manifold only coincide exactly at that point p where it is defined, but at a physical level we can admit a certain interval of error and assume that in a small neighbourhood of the point p the tangent space is a good approximation of the manifold. It is possible to work in a wide framework of arbitrary manifolds in different coordinates. A very useful example of what a manifold is, is the Earth. We know widely that it is a sphere that has a curved surface, but locally, we never perceive this curvature, it seems flat to us. Checkmate, flat-earthers!

Differential operators in , covariant derivative.

It is possible to define vectors, operators and tensors in the tangent spaces of each manifold. The explicit expression of these entities will not be shown here; it will only be mentioned that they can be described in any coordinate systems that admit a general change of the type . But careful! It will only be possible to describe them in the tangent spaces since these are the vector spaces in which we are accustomed to work. So now a problem arises for us with derivatives, or in a general way with differential operators.

If any reader remembers their stage in high school, they will without doubt remember that a derivative was defined from a limit. This limit compared a function (or a vector in a general way) evaluated at a point p and at a point very close to p, which we will call q. The usual example that is taken is to imagine a car at full speed heading towards a curve. If it does not have the intention of braking, on reaching the curve it will go off in a straight line through it; here we find the derivative of this curve, which can be an arbitrary function f(x). But what happens if I want to take a derivative on a manifold? I cannot construct the previous example on the manifold since if I move a little away from the point where I have defined my tangent space I will no longer be in the same vector space and I will not be able to take this limit in a mathematically correct way.

The limit, therefore, will not be well defined. It is here where a new concept of derivative arises, the covariant derivative, in Einstein notation:

The derivative was never so complicated.

In spite of how strange the previous expression may seem, the key resides in two terms. The first makes reference to the good old partial derivative. Yes, those that they forced you to learn to do by heart in high school. The second is a term that we denominate non-tensorial since it depends on each point and on the chosen coordinates. What we are doing is comparing two vectors belonging to the same space . One is the one that we already had in the tangent space generated by q and the other is a resulting image that comes from the vector that lived in the space of p, but that has been parallel transported to the tangent space generated by q. This parallel transport is given to us by the factor .

Probably you, who were quietly enjoying this marvellous day, will be politely cursing me in all possible languages. I came to discover general relativity, and they bring me a story of weird derivatives, of curved spaces and a nomenclature that much more resembles Kafkaesque vocabulary! I ask you then for patience; these concepts will be necessary to understand surprising aspects much later. But since I owe myself exclusively to your understanding almost to perfection what I try to transmit to you, it is my obligation to give you a simple example.

A simple(?) example.

The key of the concept of this new derivative resides in that we need to compare two objects that, a priori, live in spaces that are not comparable. Let us make a simile with monetary quantities: Let us imagine that you earn some five euros per hour here in Spain for a certain job, but your odious cousin James, the one who is always reminding you how happy he is living in the United States, tells you that he earns 6.04 US dollars per hour and for the same job. Obviously he does not miss the opportunity to call you and vilely rub it in your face. But you, who know well and are knowledgeable about differential geometry and covariant derivatives, explain to your cousin the fact that he is mistaken, that he cannot crudely compare dollars with euros, since they belong to different monetary systems.

If he wanted to do it properly, he should transport the dollars to euros, along an (imaginary) path that would transform one quantity into the other, and he would realise that, when he could compare both quantities in euros, both earn exactly the same. The dollars are the vector in the space of p, the euros, that of the space of q, the path from dollars to euros is the parallel transport that makes it possible for us to work with a vector in q, which essentially comes from the one that existed in p, in the same way that 5 euros and 6.04 US dollars represent the same thing, only expressed in different systems.

Understanding the curvature of space.

Future plans.

Throughout this article we have talked about two fundamental concepts of differential geometry, which are manifolds and the covariant derivative. These two objects, although tedious when it comes to explaining them, are fundamental for what we will define in the next instalment. It is one of the most important objects for describing curved spaces, the Riemann tensor. This tensor will be fundamental to be able to understand Einstein’s equations, so don’t miss it. Until next time, thinking minds!

The Riemann tensor, the holy grail of differential geometry.

Mathematical identification of curvature.

Several weeks ago we were talking about differential geometry. Surely you remember that somewhat tedious article. Probably, at some moment of its reading, the reader reconsidered the real importance of giving so many formal definitions. The answer today is clear: there is no doubt, all that context was necessary in order to be able to define now one of the most famous tensors of all geometry, the Riemann tensor. This is related to the concept of curvature and arises from comparison once again. But this time not of vectors, but of covariant derivatives. This “comparison” between operators, if the mathematicians allow me to call it that, is called a commutator and is defined in the form:

In our concrete case, if we apply this quantity to a vector, we will be measuring, so to speak, the difference existing between a vector travelling one path and travelling another. When we do, then, this calculation, we obtain the following:

The manifestation of curvature with the Riemann tensor.

In the previous expression there appear the Riemann tensor on one side, and the torsion tensor on the other. The fundamental idea is that this is how the concept of curvature appears in a natural way, reflected in that taking two different paths in a curved space leads us to a difference in the final state of the vectors that have travelled each path. This does not occur in flat space, where if we transport two vectors these always point to the same place independently of the path that they travel. This non-flat geometry is made manifest with the Riemann tensor, an extremely important object for the later deduction of Einstein’s equations.

Curvature is not something as trivial as it seems.

Parallel transport in a curved space, a very subtle concept.

It is worth stopping for a moment to explain in greater detail what this business is of curvature arising naturally from parallel transport. It will be easy for you, my friend, who have four long-suffering years of university degree behind you! With great reason the reader could reproach me. In case it served as consolation, I could answer that four years in the physics degree are of little use when we want to go deep into the great theories developed by the human being. But we can indeed approach their understanding. Let us highlight simple examples as the main methodology to be able to understand more complex ideas. Let us begin with something simple: what does it mean for something to be curved?

Curvature… curvature is you.

Whenever we think of something curved the first image that comes to our mind is that of a ball. Great, we have already come across a visual image of what we want to understand. But we are going to go a little further. Let us imagine that we could transport a needle over the whole surface of the ball without it getting punctured. If initially our needle were found at one of the poles of the ball, pointing upwards, and we had the audacity to “transport” (watch out, here the concept already appears) this needle as far as, for example, the equator of this ball, would the reader say that it is pointing in the same direction in which it did initially? Of course not! It is directed towards a direction that keeps 45º with the initial one. If we broke the ball and spread its fabric over the floor of our house, what do you think would happen then with the direction of the needle? Surprisingly nothing, it keeps pointing and will keep doing so upwards, however much parallel transport you wanted to give it.

The curvature of the universe and of the beach ball.

In the same way as the beach ball, our space-time also presents curvature, and that non-coincidence of the vectors (call it a needle for the visual example) on performing a parallel transport on them is reflected in that taking two different paths will not lead us to the same vector. This is shown mathematically in the two previously mentioned tensors. This idea related to geometry is extremely important, since it describes for us the physical as well as mathematical nature of space-time. There exist some variants of the Riemann tensor, the so-called “contractions” of it, which are simply objects that arise from the restriction of the number of components that it has. One of the most important is the Ricci tensor, defined as:

(†)

This tensor we do write explicitly, since it will be of great importance when it comes to elaborating Einstein’s equations and we will make use of it again in coming chapters.

The Levi-Civita connection.

We need one more clue.

The formalism developed up to here has been of great beauty, but for that avid reader there will be something that still does not add up for them; there is something that has still not been revealed, some clue is still missing to build the complete puzzle. And it turns out that objects of the type (†) are very pretty, but does anyone really know what form they have? The answer is that there is not a unique answer. Since they are non-tensorial objects, that is, that depend on the chosen coordinates, there exists a great variety of ways of fixing them. But for our study there is one that takes the prize, the so-called Levi-Civita connection.

Connected with space-time.

This is perhaps the least formal part of this series, since obtaining the exact form of (†) is an arduously complex job, even for a humble student like me. These objects are related to the metric of space in the form:

(†)

This connection allows us to relate completely all the cards of our deck. This is how our fundamental curvature tensors are related in the last instance to the metric of space, which is the object that describes its geometric properties. Besides, due to the properties of this connection, the torsion tensor disappears from the calculation mentioned before for the curvature. Now it is the Riemann tensor that carries all the weight of the curvature. The problem is now closed and compact; all that remains is to establish the general interpretation of the physics of space-time in order to be able to arrive at Einstein’s equations.

Bibliography.

  • Notes on General Relativity (Apuntes de Relatividad General). Bert Janssen. University of Granada.
  • Gravitation. D.D. Ivanenko, G.A Sardanashvili.
  • The Evolution of Physics. Albert Einstein, Leopoldo Infeld.

Discovering particle physics.

Recently there has been published in one of the most prestigious scientific journals, Physical Review Letter, the first data obtained from the experiment called Muon g-2 at the high-energy laboratory Fermilab (FLAB) (in honour of the physicist Enrico Fermi), located in Batavia, a city situated some 50 km from Chicago in the USA. This publication has caused more stir than is usually expected because it has hit squarely the current theory that governs particle physics, the standard model (Standard Model, SM for its initials in English). This theory, among other things, describes the interactions between the fundamental particles. One of these fundamental particles is the lepton , which is precisely the one that brings us today to this article. But before going into the technical parts of the results obtained by Fermilab, we are going to explain briefly what such a mysterious particle this is.

The muon, an overweight electron.

For practical purposes the title of this section should not alarm us, since the muon shares many properties with the electron, a particle that perhaps does ring a bell for you. But one of the properties that it does not share is that it is a particle whose mass is bigger. Within the standard model there exists a set of particles called leptons, mentioned previously. These particles are currently distributed in the SM in three families or generations, displayed in figure 1. Here we see how the muon is a particle with a mass of some 105.7 MeV/c², some 200 times bigger than that of the electron.

Figure 1: Image where the fundamental particles of the standard model are observed. The three generations of particles are observed and how the leptons are the ones painted in green. This image has a Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 3.0 Unported licence. The author is Buckminsterfullereno C60 and the URL of the image is specified in the bibliography.

The key to the enigma, the magnetic moment of the muon.

Having briefly expounded the general lines that describe the SM and having identified the muon within this theory, we proceed to focus on one of the characteristics that we will need to understand the recent experiment. The magnetic moment of the muon (as of many other particles) consists of a physical quantity that describes the response of this particle when an external magnetic field appears. With this quantity it is possible to calculate the energy or the force that the field exerts on the particle, among other things. The magnetic moment is related to the spin (†) of the particle and is described by the equation:

The key of the recently published work is the value of the quantity (†), which is where the measurement that has been made is centred. Here is where we are going to find the main problem that the data throw up: they contradict the theory.

New physics in the experiment on the muon.

Now we have all the ingredients necessary to be able to understand briefly at a simple level what it is that has happened with the publication of the data taken by Fermilab. The standard model theoretically predicted [4] a value for (†) of:

(†)

Equation 3.

Do not let the reader worry about the term ppm (for its initials in English, part per million), since it makes reference to the precision with which a quantity is measured. The only thing that you do have to keep in mind is that the Fermilab experiment has managed to improve the precision when it comes to calculating this quantity. The value given has been:

Equation 4

This result throws up a difference from the value predicted by the standard model of (†). Do not let the reader be frightened either; this jargon is used to give a level of statistical significance to our data [7]. The only thing that must be kept in mind is that a discovery is usually considered when the difference between what is predicted and what is measured reaches, as a minimum, (†). Well then, if the result of equation (4) is joined with the value obtained by another experiment from some years ago, the BNL E821, a value of (†) is obtained that differs from the predicted value by (†). This result induces us to think that there may exist more physics behind the standard model! The schematic image of the anomaly is represented in figure (2).

Figure 2: Image obtained from [5]. The range for the values that would be attainable within the predictions of the standard model and the range for the measurements of the FLAB and BNL E821 experiments are observed. It can be seen how the difference between both quantities is the one already mentioned.

Conclusions.

The main conclusion that the reader should keep, however much it hurts me, is not to get too enthusiastic. With this type of measurements one has to be very cautious and have a lot of patience. Science is like that. It is true that a surprising result has been obtained, with a difference of (†), but we still need many more data and experiments to affirm that there has been a failure in the predictions of the standard model. For more information and research on the technical part of the experiment see [5], which is the original publication, or the summary video given by FLAB [3].

The importance of the equivalence principle.

Background.

During the last months we have travelled together through this fascinating world of general relativity. We have tried to approach, as a first approximation, all the ideas and concepts, arduously complex, that the theory encompasses. We already talked about them in previous chapters of this series. Today we probably bring the most important concept of this whole development. The equivalence principle, which Einstein himself admitted was “the best idea he had had in his life”, appears as a bridge between special relativity and general relativity, where we try to unite all the aspects of the four-dimensional Minkowski space in a theory that takes into account the gravitational field and non-inertial observers.

Equivalence between inertial mass and gravitational mass.

One of the bases for understanding this idea that we will try to show resides, no more and no less, in Newtonian mechanics itself. In it, there appear two clearly differentiated terms: the inertial mass on one side, and the gravitational mass on the other. To make ourselves a simple image of what each one is, we could say that the inertial mass is the one that appears in a natural way in Newton’s second law. On the other hand, the gravitational mass is the one that appears in Newton’s law of Universal Gravitation. Both appear as a constant of proportionality. In the first case, the mass has a meaning linked to the very inertia of the body, to the resistance that it puts up to changing its state of motion. In the second case, the mass is what originates the gravitational force, since it is this that originates the gravitational field. In spite of their clear conceptual difference, experience tells us that both are worth exactly the same.

The equivalence principle in homogeneous fields.

Einstein’s idea.

In this article we will focus on homogeneous fields, where the gravitational field is approximately constant, as can happen, for example, on the surface of the Earth. Afterwards we will extend it to more general fields. Einstein always tried to elaborate a theory where gravity had a place. This aspiration was joined to the fact that he was always surprised by the result that we comment above, the equivalence between the inertial mass and the gravitational mass. For him, this result kept a much deeper truth hidden in nature. When the idea of the equivalence principle came into his head, he imagined it starting from a fact, “a priori”, quite intuitive: an observer in free fall (he is accelerated) does not feel his own weight. This implies that for himself, he could think that in reality he was situated in a region of space where there was no gravitational field. From here the statement of this principle is deduced:

An observer in free fall in a (constant) gravitational field is equivalent to an inertial observer in the absence of gravity.

Bert Janssen, General Theory of Relativity, University of Granada (Spain)

Gravity, an illusion created by our coordinate system?

The equivalence principle that we have mentioned also admits another statement in the case of constant accelerations; it says:

An observer in uniformly accelerated motion is equivalent to an observer in a constant gravitational field.

Bert Janssen, General Theory of Relativity, University of Granada (Spain)

This principle can find a simple meaning if we make use of the basic kinematics equations that we saw in high school. If we remember, free fall for a stone was described by the equation

but if we perform a change of coordinates of the type

we realise that the resulting equation is

that is, that equation that describes for us a body moving in an inertial way, that is, at constant velocity. In this way what we find is that, really, gravity can be interpreted as an artefact that arises from the choice of our coordinates. In physics, this type of forces are called fictitious forces, like the Coriolis force. One must take into account that all the time we have been referring to systems where the gravitational field is constant; in the general case it will not be so trivial, but it is important that one has this idea of what seems an illusion in the case of the gravitational force.

The equivalence principle in inhomogeneous fields. Implications.

The equivalence principle, a local property.

In the general case in which the gravitational field is no longer constant, the equivalence principle admits a slightly different and subtle idea: we begin to speak of locality. The statement of the principle is shown thus:

Observers in free fall in a general gravitational field are locally equivalent to inertial observers.

Bert Janssen, General Theory of Relativity, University of Granada (Spain)

Now this principle acquires a local property: it is fulfilled only in certain regions of space-time, where the scales are “small”. By small or local we refer essentially to those zones of space-time where the tidal effects are not perceived, or to the precision of the experiments used in our measurements. This is not a circular argument; it is not a safe-conduct that leads us to an I cannot say anything about where I cannot make good measurements. This entails a much deeper understanding of the physics behind the nature of the gravitational field. Two particles with equal charge but with different mass will not have the same acceleration impelled by an electric field

(†)

something that does not occur with the gravitational field, where two particles with different mass will indeed have the same acceleration, because of the nature of the equivalence of the inertial mass and the gravitational mass, which we were talking about in the first section of this post:

(†)

Thus, the gravitational acceleration is the same for particles with the same mass and it shows us that the equivalence principle contains at a deep level much more physics than we could expect.

The equivalence principle in a mathematical context.

Probably this is one of the most important sections that have followed in this series. In it we are going to give a general vision of what the equivalence principle implies mathematically and we will see the connection that this has with the part of differential geometry expounded in previous sections. The fundamental conclusion that arises from the equivalence principle is that at any point of curved space-time we have a transformation of coordinates that locally makes us able to be in a Minkowski space. It is a locally flat space-time, a property that fits perfectly with the definition of differential manifold that we gave previously. Thus, we arrive at a fundamental fact: Space-time is a four-dimensional Lorentzian differential manifold whose curvature is completely determined by the Levi-Civita connection. Free particles in this four-dimensional space-time follow the trajectories of the geodesics given in it. Due to the inhomogeneity of space-time there appear deviations between these trajectories. This is how the analogy arises between the physics of Einstein and that of Newton. What for Newton is the equation of a particle affected by a gravitational force

(†)

for Einstein is nothing more than the equation of a geodesic in a curved space

(†)

where the Newtonian gravitational force is nothing more than a fictitious force that arises from the choice of coordinates of the system. Thus one arrives at a surprising implication: gravity is purely geometry.

Background to the equations of gravity.

Everything we have learned.

During the last months we have been reviewing the main concepts of Einstein’s general relativity. We have talked about the historical context that precedes it, differential manifolds, differential geometry and about the equivalence principle. All of them have served us to have a global image of what space-time really is and how we can understand the gravitational field and force. Now it is the moment to deduce Einstein’s original equations.

Physical interpretation of the energy-momentum tensor.

A tensor that is going to appear in a natural way in Einstein’s equations is the so-called energy-momentum tensor. This is because up to now we have arrived at the conclusion that gravity appears as a consequence of the curvature of space-time, but we have not talked about what produces this curvature. The source of the gravitational field is nothing more than the mass of the object, which, in turn, is nothing more than one of the manifestations of its energy (remember ). It is therefore that when we work with large magnitudes, be it systems of many particles, fields, or, in general, a set of matter, it is usual to treat the joint system as a fluid. Said fluid contains information about the energy density in each one of its directions, as well as it can also contain information about the pressure, temperature,… etc. The tensor that takes care of describing these characteristics is called the energy-momentum tensor.

Mathematical structure of the energy-momentum tensor.

Once we have understood more or less where the idea of the energy-momentum tensor arises from, we are going to see what its mathematical structure is like. In general it is usually denoted as . The physical definition of this tensor is usually supported on the fact that what it shows is the flux of the momenta through a surface . This is nothing more than the generalisation of a current vector as it appears for example in Maxwell’s equations. The simplest example of energy-momentum tensor is the one that is denominated cold matter, and that describes a set of particles that do not interact; it has the form

Einstein’s equations.

Mathematical and physical restrictions for the deduction of Einstein’s equations.

Consequences of Einstein’s equations.

As we see, the problem of general relativity is reduced to the expression expounded above. This equation keeps within itself a brutal amount of information. It is a system of ten partial differential equations, non-linear and coupled, of second order in the metric (†). This makes the resolution of this equation really very complicated. Einstein himself was aware of this fact, and believed that he would never manage to find a solution for his equations. To his surprise, the following year the first solution to his equations was found, the Schwarzschild solution, the simplest for a spherically symmetric mass distribution. Among other things, this solution is capable of describing, in first approximation, cosmological objects such as the Sun or a black hole itself.

Conclusions and author’s note.

During this brief series we have made a general review of the main concepts of general relativity. Take into account that many subtle characteristics, details and mathematical formulations have been overlooked so as not to extend said series into excessive complications. An attempt has been made to find the balance between the correct formalism of the theory and the qualitative explanation of the most complicated ideas. In many books, among others those that have been mentioned in this bibliography, these topics are delved into in a much deeper way. For any query, I will be willing to answer questions and even debate about certain topics for anyone who wants to. I hope you have enjoyed this journey as much as I have.

The other day, during a brief rest on the balcony of my house, I was left astounded by the sunset that was taking place before me. The rays of our beloved star were seen scattered by the atmosphere and drew a pretty landscape that was worthy of seeing. At that moment, I remembered how important electromagnetic theory was and had been in the development of human history. The whole formalism of this theory was summarised in four beautiful equations. Today we are going to try to shed light on this topic which, even being extremely important, one never really gets to know what it consists of. Today we talk about Maxwell’s equations.

James Clerk Maxwell, a brief introduction about the father of electromagnetism.

Maxwell in his childhood and during university.

Little Maxwell was born in Edinburgh, on a 13th of June of 1831. He did not have an easy childhood; he lost his mother at 8 years of age [2]. At school he was not accepted for a long time and suffered from a severe social isolation. This loneliness ended when he met those who would be his lifelong friends, Lewis Campbell and Peter Guthrie Tait. After his stage of initial studies, where he attended the Edinburgh Academy, he went on to enter his university years. He began his studies at the prestigious University of Cambridge, to end up completing them at that of Edinburgh.

Take life more calmly, Mr Maxwell.

It turns out that the young Scot did not want to waste time. From a very young age he stood out for his curiosity and his logical and mathematical capacities. At 18 years of age he published his first two works in the Royal Society of Edinburgh [1]. If our reader turns out to be a young person, do not throw your hands up to your head. You have to take into account that Maxwell was one of those scientists who appear once (if there is luck) every century. After finishing his studies and, overcoming the also premature death of his father, he ended up working as professor of Natural Philosophy at Marischal College in Aberdeen in 1856. From here, the most fruitful years of his career would come. In 1858 he married Katherine Mary Dewar and, two years later, he accepted a post as professor at King’s College London.

Maxwell’s equations, a mathematical adventure.

Once we have briefly reviewed some aspects of his life up to his arrival at university, we are going to go into what really interests us in this article. We are going to talk about the equations that bear his name and that constitute the bases of classical electromagnetism. In this article we will focus on the vacuum equations, which make their understanding much easier.

Stopping briefly at the concept of field.

Before formally introducing Maxwell’s equations, we must insist on understanding the concept of field. A field is a function that endows each point of space with a concrete characteristic (if it is scalar, a number; if it is vectorial, a vector). This is a concept that broke with the way of thinking of the time, very influenced by Newtonian dynamics. Now forces arise as a manifestation of the field that a source of it creates. In the electromagnetic case, one of the sources can be a charge. The concept of source is also quite interesting and we will understand it completely when we see the equations one by one.

Maxwell’s equations.

Without further delay, we are going to finally show the original equations that are attributed to J. Clerk Maxwell. These equations in vacuum are shown as:

(†)

(†)

(†)

(†)

It is very important to understand that these four equations, at bottom, are only telling us about the sources of the two fields, of the electric field (†) and of the magnetic field (†). These sources are obtained from the mathematical operations of the curl (†) and of the divergence (†), indicating the vector and scalar sources of a generic field (†).

Maxwell’s equations, physical interpretation.

First and second Maxwell equations, the sources of the electric field.

The first two equations tell us about the sources of the electric field. When we speak of sources, we must understand it as that which generates the field that we are considering. In this case, these two equations make reference to the scalar sources and to the vector sources. We see then that the scalar sources of the electric field are the charge densities, or if we prefer, the charges that there are in a certain region of space. What the first equation tells us is that, when we are in the presence of a (positive) charge, field lines are created that come out of it. With negative charges the opposite occurs; into these the electric field enters. A schematic example of the scalar sources of the electric field can be observed in figure 1. Positive charges behave as sources and negative charges as sinks [3]. In the case of the second equation, it tells us geometrically how much the field rotates around a point. In vacuum, this vector part of the electric field is generated by the temporal variation of the magnetic field, what is usually known as Faraday’s induction equation.

Figure 1. The field lines that positive (left) and negative (right) charge distributions generate are shown. This image has a Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0 International licence.

Second and third Maxwell equations, the sources of the magnetic field.

Having more or less understood the idea of the scalar and vector sources of the fields, this section can now be understood more quickly. The scalar sources of the magnetic field are… none. What a surprise, right? Well yes, to this day we still do not have experimental evidence that the scalar sources of the magnetic field are different from zero. As a consequence of this one has that magnetic monopoles do not exist in nature. Although, if you want, we can talk about that another day. On the other hand, the vector sources of the magnetic field are the currents (†) that appear in a certain region of space. That is, charges in motion. An example of the field lines generated by a magnet can be seen in figure 2. Another source of the magnetic field is the temporal variation of the electric field. This last term, moreover, is of relative importance, since without it the continuity equation of charge was not fulfilled [3].

Figure 2. The magnetic field lines are shown. If the reader notices, they can understand why this field does not have scalar sources: in terms of Gauss’s law, the lines of this field are closed and never net-cut a surface giving a net flux different from zero. This image has a Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 4.0 International licence.

Conclusions.

Maxwell’s equations were one of the great milestones in the history of science. For the first time the concept of field was used in a consolidated way, which would mark the beginning of the later development that led us to current scientific knowledge. Nowadays all electronic devices, even the one by means of which you are reading this article, work on the bases of these four equations. Many physical and mathematical aspects can be obtained from the understanding of what the young Maxwell devised in his day. In this article it was not taken into account, but these equations admit a covariant form. The theory can also be quantised and electromagnetic interactions can be explained by means of what is called QED (Quantum Electrodynamics). All this, if time and experience allow us, we will try to develop in future articles. Let us trust that Maxwell could be proud of everything that we have learned.

item.content:encoded:
Reading time: 6 minutes

Without doubt one of the most interesting particles that describe our universe are neutrinos. These particles have some very interesting properties. So much so that nowadays, understanding what the phenomenology existing in them is like is one of the main objectives for many particle physicists. Their very existence has put the Standard Model in check several times and, in fact, it continues doing so to this day.

Understanding neutrino physics.

Neutrinos, the origin of the enigma.

It was the year 1930 when the Austrian physicist Wolfram Pauli postulated for the first time the existence of such exotic particles. His postulate arises as the solution to a problem that had been posed with decays. The problem resided in that such processes did not conserve the energy and the linear momentum of all the particles involved. To solve this, Pauli proposed that there must exist a particle without mass, without charge and that did not interact strongly either. That is why it was not until almost 20 years later, when Clyde Cowan and Frederick Reines demonstrated its existence experimentally, that there was complete certainty that neutrinos were really there in those processes.

But, what really are neutrinos?

Formally, neutrinos are defined as a type of particle that is included within the set of leptons. As was already mentioned in a later article, where we were talking about the experimental results of the Fermilab muon g2, the muon is also a lepton. As it could not be otherwise, in the original standard model there exists the muon neutrino, together with its two first cousins, the electron one and the tau one. Together they form the three flavour states that exist in the current theoretical framework and that can be observed in the previously used figure 1.

Figure 1: Image where the fundamental particles of the standard model are observed. The three generations of particles are observed and how the leptons are the ones painted in green. This image has a Creative Commons Attribution-Share Alike 3.0 Unported licence. The author is Buckminsterfullereno C60 and the URL of the image is specified in the bibliography.

It is important to mention that these particles interact with practically nothing. In fact, this makes the experiments that are carried out with them quite complicated from a technical point of view. Right now you are being crossed by thousands and thousands of neutrinos that come from, among other sources, our Sun.

The problems begin: neutrino oscillation.

Oscillating was never so much fun.

It turns out that one of the main properties of these particles is that they are capable of oscillating between some flavour states and others. This means that, for example, initially we can have an electron neutrino state and, after travelling a certain distance, obtain a muon neutrino. This fact became manifest with experiments as important as the one carried out in the USA, the Homestake experiment. In it, only 1/3 of the expected electrons were detected. What happened? The reality is that the experiment was designed to measure only electron neutrinos. Of the initial ones that came out of the Sun, only 1/3 were detected because the remaining part had oscillated to the other two families of the standard model. This phenomenon meant a problem that the scientists of the end of the 20th century had to deal with. The answer, nothing further from reality, consisted of a base mistake: neutrinos do really have mass.

The mass of neutrinos.

The fundamental fact of why these particles oscillate is because each one of the flavour states is constructed, in reality, by a linear combination of three mass states. This fact is astonishing. As the mass states are different (some weigh more than others), the velocity with which they propagate through space is different for the three mass states. The most intuitive way of understanding this is to see neutrinos as waves following the formulation of quantum mechanics. Each mass state produces a wave that propagates in space at a different velocity. This makes the composition of the three, at a determined moment, able to give a concrete flavour state. But after a time or a distance has elapsed, this composition can give rise to a different total resulting wave, the one characteristic of another flavour state of the neutrino.

There is a solution for (almost) everything.

Place of neutrinos in the current standard model.

The fact is that the existence of neutrino oscillation and the later proposal of their mass states made the foundations of the standard model tremble. It does not predict the existence of the mass of neutrinos. That is why over the years attempts have been made to give answers to the reason for this fact, above all from a vision of quantum field theory. Mass terms are not easy to include in this theory, since they do not usually respect the rest of the symmetries. One possibility is to consider what are called Majorana neutrinos, where the mass term is related not only to the field of the neutrino, but also to its complex conjugate.

The future in neutrino experiments.

Many are the challenges that still remain to be answered. From a theoretical point of view, one has to keep looking for the way for the standard model to be capable of predicting the masses of neutrinos. At an experimental level, new neutrino oscillation experiments are being fine-tuned, such as SBND or DUNE. In them an attempt is made to give an answer to some anomalies in the data that have been obtained in different experiments over the years. These anomalies suggest that there could exist a fourth neutrino mass state, instead of the three that we have mentioned. What is clear is that there is still a long way to go until managing to completely understand the nature of these so mysterious particles.

The Short Baseline Neutrino program (SBN) is one of the experiments that may break particle physics in the coming years. A few weeks ago we were talking about a type of very characteristic particles of the universe which we call neutrinos. In this new post I seek to bring the general public closer to a type of physics that is usually abandoned in the academic stage but that is as important as, or more than, the one that is usually taught in it. We are talking about experimental physics, and in particular experimental particle physics. For this we are going to talk about the work that is carried out in one of the most important research centres in the world, Fermilab. We will also understand what measuring neutrino oscillations consists of, at a technical level. If you want to have today a closer idea of what is really done in physics, stay with us.

Doing real experimental physics at the SBN.

Experimental physics in the Fermilab laboratory.

The first thing we are going to do is to have a brief introduction about where Fermilab is located and what it is. It is a high-energy laboratory situated in the city of Batavia, some 50 km from the city of Chicago. In it diverse experiments related to particle physics are carried out, and in particular the Short Baseline Neutrino Program has been launched, which hopes to be able to test the hypothesis of the sterile neutrino. It is about this program that we are going to talk today, and the one that we will use as a reference to be able to understand some concepts of experimental physics.

Brief idea of what the sterile neutrino consists of.

The sterile neutrino, which is the particle that sustains the main line of research of the SBN, is a type of hypothetical particle that could break with the bases of the current standard model. It is a massive neutrino (with respect to the rest of the neutrinos of the standard model) that interacts, “a priori”, only by means of the gravitational force. The hypothesis of the existence of this particle arises from the fact that for several years, different neutrino oscillation experiments have reported different anomalies in their results. These anomalies indicated a possible existence of a fourth neutrino mass state to which the rest of the families of the standard model oscillated. Its existence is not yet proven and that is why new, increasingly sensitive experiments are being sought, such as the SBN.

In experimental physics you have to use your head, the particular case of the SBN.

And it is that it is not so easy to detect a particle that interacts with practically nothing. For this a very broad technological and technical effort is needed. In the SBN liquid argon time projection chambers are used, usually denoted by LAr-TPCs. These chambers are capable of giving information about the different events that take place when the particles arrive at the detector. On the other hand, to ensure the reliability of and commitment to the experiment, use is made of sensitivity studies where the capacity that it has to be able to test hypotheses to a certain degree of probability is put to the test. We will discuss both characteristics briefly throughout this article.

Phenomenology of the SBN experiment.

Liquid Argon time projection chambers as detectors of the SBN.

A liquid argon time projection chamber consists of a box full of liquid Argon, where on both sides of the box are placed an electrical terminal that performs the function of anode and another that performs the function of cathode. This technology was initially proposed by Carlo Rubia [1]. The main idea of detection arises thus: when a neutrino arrives at what is called the active volume (which is nothing more than the volume where the Liquid Argon is situated), it interacts with the argon atom. When they collide, a set of charged particles is produced; these charged particles ionise the rest of the atoms of the volume. The electrons that arise from these ionisations are dragged by means of an electric field to our detectors. Thus we obtain a kind of trace that these particles have followed after the collision. This allows us to calculate properties such as the momentum or the mass. A very illustrative image of this functioning can be found in an interactive video developed by Fermilab [2].

Sensitivity studies at the SBN: Simulation of the experiment’s data.

To understand what the sensitivity analyses of the detectors consist of, we must first understand how one works in the field of experimental particle physics. If we want to demonstrate the sensitivity of a detector, first we must make a simulation of what we expect to obtain after a period of several years of data taking. For this we will make use of the data published in the 2015 proposal [3]. What is obtained is something like that of figure 1, for one of the detectors of the program.

Figure 1: Expected events for the far detector ICARUS T600 (right). Each one of the colours is associated with a different type of event that is expected. In the different shades of green the charged current (CC) events for the electron neutrinos are observed. In orange are the events related to photons and in purple the CC events but where muon neutrinos appear. These data that are shown are the result of the study in the appearance channel.

Once these figures are obtained, one proceeds to obtain something similar to that of figure 2. In this, what is done is to oscillate the obtained events within one theoretical framework or another, in our case in that where the oscillation of the sterile neutrino is taken into account. In this way we now count on all the data to put the sensitivity of our experiment to the test.

Figure 2: The events explored in figure 1 are shown together with a new data set related to the name Signal and which make reference to the oscillation signal that we would have if we considered an oscillation within the theoretical framework where the sterile neutrino appears. These data are oscillated for the ICARUS T600 detector in the appearance channel.

Sensitivity studies at the SBN: Mathematics applied to the experiment.

Once one has the necessary data from which to start, what is carried out is a sensitivity study making use of statistics. For this concrete case of experiment what is called the likelihood function is constructed, which is a probability function in a two-dimensional parameter space. The two main parameters are those that are called the mixing angle (†) and (†), and they serve to characterise the physical properties of the neutrino. This function is expressed by equation 1 and gives us an idea of how far our hypothesis model (sterile neutrino) ( (†)) is going to stray from the current framework, the three-family framework ( (†)).

[Equation 1 — not rendered in the source PDF]

In a one-dimensional analogy (although it should not be understood strictly) this function can act as a chi-squared and basically we use it, repeating myself again, to test a certain hypothesis. Once it is constructed, what is usually done is to draw the lines at and (†) together with allowed zones of the parameters obtained from global fits of other studies [6], [7]. Something similar to that of figure 3 is obtained [4].

Figure 3: Final sensitivity study in the appearance channel. We see how the mentioned lines are represented together with the most probable regions of the parameters. In the image allowed regions for the LSND experiment are also included.

I will not extend myself on the explanation of what the and (†) mean; I will only say that it has to do with the capacity to measure a point sufficiently far from the mean and with a certain probability that this is not due to statistical fluctuations, but rather to there being something that is not considered in our theoretical model. For more information, I found a very interesting post on the blog of Francis R. Villatoro, which I strongly recommend, that deals with this topic [5].

Conclusions.

The interpretation of figure 3 may turn out to be complicated for anyone who is not familiar with these topics. But I assure you that as soon as we comment on a couple of details it will turn out easier for you than learning to multiply was in its day. The lines that we have drawn at “x” sigmas are bounding the parameter space to the zone where the detector can measure things (from the line towards the right of the plot). If the most probable zones (green) fall within this allowed zone, then the experiment is a great candidate to be able to test the hypothesis that is needed. This is, for example, how the construction of experiments is justified from an experimental point of view. And however much it hurts us, the investments that are received externally have to be justified! I hope the reader has enjoyed this unusual article; for more, do not hesitate to ask me through my social networks or by commenting on this post.

Until now we had never dedicated any post throughout our short existence to solid-state physics. This discipline constitutes one of the hottest topics within current physics, with numerous advances day after day. Today I want to talk to you about the Drude model, one of the simplest models posed for the description of metals.¹

Dissecting the Drude model.

Drude runs into the first problems.

The description of metals is not something trivial at first sight. We must make an effort of comprehension and understand that a few centuries ago there were no concrete notions of the quantum world. That is why Drude must face this problem without a clear idea of what the internal behaviour of electrons consists of using quantum-mechanical concepts. Due to this, the model is posed from a purely classical vision, where there are some assumptions that really lack a somewhat more solid foundation. Even so, the model continues being a good tool when it comes to describing qualitatively what occurs inside the metal. Also for having an idea in first approximation that later makes us go deeper into the understanding of its internal functioning.

Main assumptions of the Drude model.

That said, the Drude model starts from some main assumptions [1]:

  1. Between collisions the electrons are not affected by the fields that the ions (atoms with positive charge) produce (free electron approximation) or by the other electrons within the metal (independent electron approximation). That is, in the absence of any external field, the electrons after a collision would follow a straight line. In the case of the existence of an introduced external field, the equation of motion would be described by Newton’s second law.
  2. Collisions in the Drude model alter the velocity of the electrons in an instantaneous and abrupt way. Drude moreover considers that this collision is produced against the so-called cores (electron cores) of the metal. The cores are the structures composed of the electrons bound to the ion that are not free. A schematic image is observed in figure 1.
  3. There exists a very important parameter of this model, the so-called relaxation time (†). This gives us an idea of the mean time that an electron takes to come out of one collision and arrive at another. This will be useful to us when it comes to calculating, among other things, the conductivity predicted by the model and the Lorenz number.
  4. The last assumption is perhaps the least intuitive. It turns out that the Drude model assumes that after each collision, the electron acquires a new velocity that is only related directly to the temperature associated with the region where the collision was produced. Thus it is said that each collision maintains thermodynamic equilibrium locally.

At bottom we see that it is a very simple model where the electrons are free and the only thing that matters is the collisions with the cores. Reading time: 7 minutes

Motion in non-inertial systems is usually one of the many things that are not usually understood initially in physics. It is so important for subjects such as special relativity or general relativity. In general it shows up as a recurring problem in any calculation that we want to do using Newtonian mechanics. Today we will talk a little about it.

Understanding non-inertial reference systems.

Inertial and non-inertial reference system.

The first thing that we must do is to put ourselves in a concrete situation in order to be able to deduce all the components of the velocity and the acceleration. Let us imagine an inertial reference system (considered fixed) and another non-inertial system as shown in figure 1 [1].

Figure 1. Schematic image of two reference systems, one inertial and the other non-inertial. The different vectors that reference a point object are also schematised. This notation is the one we follow throughout the article.

The inertial reference system would be the one composed of the axes xyz and the non-inertial one by the trio XYZ. Both reference a point object. We initially assume a complete motion, that is: translation and rotation; that is why our angular velocity appears.

Velocity in non-inertial reference systems.

To obtain the velocity of the particle from the point of view of the inertial reference system, we will make use of the classical Galilean transformations. In the case of special relativity, these transformations would be the Lorentz ones. Following our example, if the point object moved jointly with our non-inertial reference system (which is rotating), its velocity would be:

This expression is general for any vector [2] and alludes to how time derivatives change in two different reference systems. Above all when one of them is rotating. If, moreover, our moving reference system had its own velocity , its complete components would be

Acceleration in non-inertial reference systems.

Once we have seen the velocity that is deduced from non-inertial systems, we are going to proceed to work with the acceleration deduced from this type of motion. In reality, this is the essential parameter that we want to calculate, since it is the one that appears in Newton’s second law. To arrive at its expression, we are simply going to take the time derivative in equation 3. This time derivative is with respect to the inertial (fixed) frame. Let us see what comes out:

Equation 4

In this way we can rewrite the acceleration as a function of all its relative components in the form

Equation 5

It is important that we can identify each of the components of the acceleration that appear here. The term makes reference to the acceleration seen from the non-inertial (moving) frame. On the other hand, is the acceleration of the reference system itself, if it had one. is the acceleration with tangential component in the rotation. Following this, is the normal or centripetal component of the acceleration. Finally, the term is usually called the Coriolis acceleration. It is important to understand that what appear in non-inertial reference systems are different components for the acceleration. Although this is so, what is usually done in many cases is to talk about fictitious forces. I have found that this normally leads to certain confusions.

Non-inertial frames and Newton’s second law.

Allusion to fictitious forces.

When we are doing a basic problem making use of classical dynamics, whatever we can do to make life easier for ourselves will be better. That is why many times, above all in the stage that precedes university, we have heard talk of fictitious forces. Don’t get frightened, we are here to solve this problem. In fact, without realising it, we have already solved it. We have already seen all the components of the acceleration that appear in a general motion. When we use our famous Newton’s second law, we want to do it with the fewest problems. For this, the ideal would be to be able to work with the acceleration itself that we see of the object, the one that its trajectory would apparently show. But if we only want to take into account this component of the acceleration, for us , what do we do with the rest? Well, very simple: we convert them into forces:

Equation 6

From here is where the fact of fictitious forces is deduced. In fact, probably the one that sounds most familiar to the young reader is the centripetal force. How many headaches this strange magnitude has brought us!

Understanding the basics: tangential and centripetal (central) component of the acceleration.

In relation to what was expounded in the previous section, there has always been a recurrently problematic topic among secondary-school students. Both I in that stage as a student and now that I have given classes have realised how badly problems where there is some type of rotation are understood. The famous centripetal acceleration! It turns out that, as usual, these concepts are usually passed over quickly and what they mean is not transmitted well. We have already talked about a very general situation. However, now we are going to try to restrict the problem a little. We are going to assume an object that simply rotates at a fixed distance from an axis of rotation. Of course, on a plane. In this way, only some components of the acceleration survive. We arrive at the tangential and normal components, with which one used to work in most exercises. Normally one was associated with the change in the modulus of the velocity (central) and the other with the change in its direction (central). Moreover, both had some very characteristic expressions that related them to other magnitudes. Figure 2 [3] shows a scheme of what we have talked about.

Figure 2. Components of the acceleration due to a circular motion. Both components have concrete expressions.

Arriving at the usual expressions to represent the acceleration in these problems is easy making use of equation 5. By no more than taking into account that the only components that survive are the already-mentioned tangential and normal. On the other hand, it must be taken into account that, for the tangential component, the angular acceleration () is always perpendicular to the vector that represents R. Then the vector product is reduced to the product of moduli . On the other hand, following the same idea, the triple product that appears for the central acceleration remains as

Equation 7

Thus we obtain the usual expression

Equation 8

A dose of reality.

This is how one works in classical mechanics with non-inertial systems. Nothing further from reality: simply Newton’s equation is affected because new components appear in the acceleration. All those gadgets that we did not understand in secondary school are not such. Apparent forces are nothing more than components of the acceleration rewritten in terms of forces. The central or centripetal acceleration is nothing but one more component of this mathematical paraphernalia. I hope that from now on the reader will always have clear what all this formalism, which is normally not very well understood, consisted of.
